title: Red or rough, what makes materials warmer?
central_proposition: The perceived warmth of a material is independently influenced by both its color and local surface roughness, with color having a quantitatively larger effect than roughness for indoor wall applications.

concept_definitions.name: Material warmth
concept_definitions.definition: Refers to how cold or warm a material feels to the touch, influenced by its thermal properties, but also by multisensory aspects like color and surface roughness.

concept_definitions.name: Roughness (material science)
concept_definitions.definition: A measure of the fine, closely-spaced random irregularities of a surface, caused by the production process.

concept_definitions.name: Waviness (material science)
concept_definitions.definition: A measure of the more widely-spaced repetitive irregularities which can result from vibration.

concept_definitions.name: Surface texture
concept_definitions.definition: Roughness and waviness together constitute surface texture.

concept_definitions.name: Roughness (architecture)
concept_definitions.definition: Refers to the overall concept of surface texture, encompassing a large range of surface irregularities.

argument_structure: The paper employs an experimental approach, consisting of a pre-study to investigate the single effects of color and roughness on perceived material warmth, followed by a main study to examine their combined effects and relative impact. Statistical analyses (ANOVA, paired comparisons, t-tests) are used to test hypotheses and quantify effects.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The study empirically demonstrates that material color and local surface roughness independently contribute to the multisensory perception of warmth. Warmer hues (red, yellow) and darker colors are perceived as warmer, while locally rough surfaces are perceived as warmer than smooth surfaces. These effects are additive, meaning they do not interact, and color's influence is quantitatively stronger than roughness's.

findings.mechanism: Different color parameters (hue, saturation, lightness) evoke distinct warmth perceptions, consistent with general color theory.
findings.quote: The repeated measures ANOVA shows a significant main effect of Color [F(5,88) = 20.4; p < 0.001; η² = 0.517].

findings.mechanism: Specific reddish and yellowish hues, combined with saturation and lightness, contribute to a warm perception.
findings.quote: For an indoor wall application, Ruby red and Mango yellow are perceived as the warmest colors from the set...

findings.mechanism: Specific bluish and achromatic hues contribute to a cold perception.
findings.quote: ...Light gray and Ice blue are the coldest colors (see Table 1 for means).

findings.mechanism: Positive correlations with a* and b* values indicate that red and yellow hues are associated with warmer perceptions.
findings.quote: For the perceived warmth of materials, positive correlations are found with both a* and b* (Pearson's r = 0.79 and r = 0.54, respectively).

findings.mechanism: Negative correlation with L* suggests darker colors are perceived as warmer and lighter colors as colder.
findings.quote: A moderate negative correlation is found between perceived warmth and lightness L* (Pearson's r = -0.48).

findings.mechanism: While not statistically significant at p<0.05 in the pre-study, the trend suggests roughness influences warmth perception.
findings.quote: No significant effect of Roughness is found in the repeated measures ANOVA [F(5,92) = 2.0; p = 0.09; η² = 0.095].

findings.antecedent: Local surface roughness (for flat materials, R01-R05)
findings.mechanism: Increasing local roughness on flat surfaces leads to a warmer perception.
findings.quote: A visual representation of the means (Fig. 5) suggests that, for flat materials (R01-R05), an increasing local roughness leads to an increasing perception of warmth.

findings.mechanism: Waviness, as distinct from local roughness, does not consistently influence warmth perception.
findings.quote: The results from the second subset (R06-R10) do not reflect a specific trend.

findings.antecedent: Material color (light gray, mango yellow, ice blue, sapphire blue)
findings.quote: The ANOVA with Color [...] shows significant main effects of both Color [F(3,101) = 54.3; p < 0.001; η² = 0.595] and Roughness [...] on the assessment of material warmth.
The ANOVA with Color [...] and Roughness [F(1,37) = 9.5; p < 0.005; η² = 0.204] on the assessment of material warmth.

findings.mechanism: The effect of roughness on material warmth is independent of the material's color and vice versa, indicating additive effects.
findings.quote: The absence of a significant interaction effect Color × Roughness [F(3,103) = 0.4; p > 0.5] illustrates that the effect of roughness on material warmth is independent of the material's color and vice versa.

findings.mechanism: Consistent with pre-study, specific hues are perceived as warmer.
findings.quote: As expected, warmer colors (mango yellow and sapphire blue) lead to a warmer overall perception than colder colors (light gray and ice blue)...

findings.mechanism: Consistent with pre-study, rough surfaces are perceived as warmer.
findings.quote: ...and rough surfaces lead to warmer perceptions than smooth surfaces (Fig. 6).

findings.antecedent: Change in material color (e.g., Light gray to Sapphire blue, with similar pre-study warmth difference as roughness)
findings.mechanism: Color has a quantitatively larger impact on warmth perception compared to roughness, even when initial differences are matched.
findings.quote: Relatively speaking, the effect of color on the perception of material warmth thus is 1.7 times larger than the effect of increasing the local roughness of a surface.

findings.antecedent: Material color (Set B: ice blue, sapphire blue)
findings.quote: A significant main effect of Color is shown [F(1,37) = 7.3; p < 0.05; η² = 0.164].
Roughness just failed to reach significance at the 0.05 level [F(1,37) = 3.8; p = 0.06; η² = 0.093].

The repeated measures ANOVA with Color (light gray, sapphire blue) and Roughness (smooth, rough) as independent variables, shows a significant main effect of both Color [F(1,37) = 16.3; p < 0.001; η² = 0.306] and Roughness [F(1,37) = 8.6; p < 0.01; η² = 0.189].

The repeated measures ANOVA with Color (light gray, sapphire blue) and Roughness (smooth, rough) as independent variables, shows a significant main effect of both Color [F(1,37) = 16.3; p < 0.001; η² = 0.306] and Roughness [F(1,37) = 8.6; p < 0.01; η² = 0.189].

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: A combination of a warm color and a warm roughness will result in high ratings for warmth.
A combination of a cold color and a cold roughness will result in the lowest ratings for warmth.
Samples with combined cold-warm stimuli will yield in-between warmth ratings.
Color and roughness will interact in terms of warmth perception (Q1).
A change in color will have a larger effect on the perception of material warmth than a comparable change in roughness (Q2).
bridge_warrants: The findings align with general color theory, which posits that specific hues (red, yellow) are perceived as warm, while others (blue, green) are perceived as cold.
The study supports the concept of multisensory integration, where visual cues (color) and haptic/visual cues (roughness) combine to form an overall perception, with vision often dominating.
The results extend previous suggestions that finely textured walls feel warmer than smooth walls, linking architectural observations to empirical data on local roughness.

The findings provide practical insights for architects and designers to manipulate perceived warmth in spaces through material selection and finishing techniques, even when radical changes in material color are not feasible.
limitations: The pre-study's color analysis had a limited number of achromatic samples.

The study could not definitively distinguish whether the effect of roughness on warmth perception was purely visual or also tactual, especially for indoor wall applications where touch frequency varies.
Material perception is context-dependent, and the results are specifically applicable to indoor wall applications.
The study did not investigate how the observed effects relate to a material's thermal properties (e.g., thermal effusivity).
The research focused on a specific base material (Inorganic Phosphate Cement) and did not explore other materials or new/unknown materials.

paper_metadata.title: The art of the stage set as a paradigm for an aesthetics of atmospheres
paper_metadata.crossref_title: The art of the stage set as a paradigm for an aesthetics of atmospheres
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Cet article dessine le contour d’une esthétique générale des ambiances (atmospheres) en mettant l’accent sur leur fabrication. De ce point de vue, l’art de la scénographie se révèle être un paradigme pour ce qui concerne les concepts principaux de la théorie des ambiances : les types d’ambiances (caractères), leur quasi-objectivité, les moyens pour produire une ambiance, le contenu émotionnel. La teneur ubiquitaire des ambiances est démontrée par la propension à tout scénographier dans notre civilisation présente : événements publics, politique, marchandises et même vie privée.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper proposes that visual and tactile material properties trigger cognitive associations and cross-modal integration, leading to the perception of warmth.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Perception of material warmth is an outcome of integrating multiple sensory cues (visual, tactile) rather than solely thermal input.
Learned associations between visual material properties (e.g., red color, rough texture) and thermal experiences contribute to the perception of material warmth.
Past physical interactions and experiences with materials influence the cognitive and affective interpretation of their visual and tactile properties, leading to perceived warmth.

stimulus_images.description: Illustrative examples of materials varying in color and texture, used to discuss their perceptual properties.
